prize_parts.citation: For incorporating firm heterogeneity into trade theory, explaining exporter selection, reallocation across firms and a new channel for the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: Heterogeneous-firm trade theory is a discovery with a clean conceptual core. Melitz (2003) explains why only some firms export, why trade liberalisation reallocates activity towards more productive firms, and how this raises aggregate productivity. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, together with his broader theoretical programme, makes the pair a coherent credit line. The framework moved the field from representative-firm industries to firm-level microdata, and it is now used in trade, macro, development and industrial organisation. After more than two decades its core predictions on exporter premia and within-industry reallocation have been tested across many countries and datasets. The 2008 prize recognised earlier new trade theory and did not cover this strand. As an economic historian I also value work that pairs new micro-level data with a model, and this literature did that. Having heard colleagues, I keep B010 first but hold it less firmly than in my opening, because B032 has the broadest cross-field support on the shortlist and a clean China-shock lineage.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely related heterogeneous-firm ideas and the empirical foundations, and they are not credited on this ballot. A Melitz-Helpman award therefore leaves some originators outside the credited names. Quantitative work also suggests that the welfare gains from selection depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity. These gains may be smaller than first claimed once the sufficient-statistics results are taken into account. Competing trade candidates (B003 and B041) could split the committee's view of the field.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B010 second and credits Melitz and Helpman, but warns that Bernard, Eaton and Kortum could be viewed as co-originators and that quantitative work suggests smaller welfare gains from selection.
responses.response: I agree that the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum antecedents are a real attribution problem, and I do not want to understate it. They are not on the ballot, so the committee can credit only listed names. Melitz (2003) is still the cleaner conceptual unit: it delivers selection, exporter thresholds and reallocation in one tractable model. On the welfare point, the sufficient-statistics results qualify how large the selection gains are, but they do not undo the discovery that firm-level facts need a heterogeneous-firm framework. I would therefore describe the contribution in the citation as selection and reallocation, and avoid claiming a specific magnitude of gains.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B032 first because the task and trade-shock designs are transparent, widely replicated and policy-relevant, and she treats Autor and Hanson as the core, with Dorn or Katz as a judgement call.
responses.response: I agree that B032 is a strong alternative and that the China-shock evidence is among the most credible quasi-experimental work on the list. It also speaks to my own interest in persistent regional damage. My hesitation is attribution. The task framework owes much to Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are not on the ballot, and Acemoglu was recognised in 2024. If B032 is chosen, I think the cleanest credit line is the trade-shock evidence for Autor, Hanson and Dorn. That differs from the Katz-inclusive version that Hjalmarsson and Teorell proposed, and it needs explicit committee discussion. I do not see B032 as weaker on science than B010. I rank B010 first mainly because its credit line is slightly easier to defend.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B010 first and treats the core as Melitz (2003) plus Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple, leaving out Redding because his work on quantitative and spatial extensions is later and more separable.
responses.response: I agree with this and with the two-person cut. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is substantial and thematically close to my regional work. That closeness is not a reason to widen the credit. It is a separable later strand, and a pair is easier to defend. I would add Fredriksson's caveat about functional-form dependence to my own and not treat the framework as settled on magnitudes.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B010 seventh, noting that the credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton and Kortum and the quantitative-trade literature is contested, and that competing claims within trade mean this strand may not be the one recognised.
responses.response: This is a fair concern about the field and not about the science. If the committee prefers the quantitative-trade lineage, B003 has a missing-Eaton problem, as Andersson and Friberg noted. B010 has a better-defined listed credit set. I would accept that trade may be recognised only once, but then the question is which strand is cleaner to credit, and I think B010 is.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the absence of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as disqualifying, or accepts Melitz and Helpman as the cleanest listed credit line.
How much the quantitative welfare-gain debate should affect the characterisation of the contribution.
Whether the committee prefers B032, which has broader opening support, and if so, whether it should be framed as trade-shock evidence only or as a combined tasks-and-trade contribution.
Whether recognising trade in this year is compatible with the committee's view of the other trade candidates (B003, B041).
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My documented connections are to Lund colleagues (including Tommy Andersson), to Johannes Lindvall, Alexandra Cermeño and the Lund economic-history school, and none is credited on any of B010, B032 or B042. My research on regional growth and local adjustment is thematically adjacent to Redding's spatial work and to the China-shock literature. That is field proximity, and I applied common criteria.
